verifiedFacts.claim: Gary Byrd co-wrote the lyrics to "Village Ghetto Land" and had labored for three months on the words before Wonder called him from the studio to say he had added another verse.

sourceRefs.extract: Gary Byrd had a particularly harrowing experience while co-writing the lyrics to the track “Village Ghetto Land.” He had labored for three months perfecting the words to what he believed to be the complete song. Then Wonder called him from the recording studio and casually informed him that he had added another verse.

sourceRefs.label: Classic Motown
sourceRefs.title: Stevie Wonder - "I Wish" | Classic Motown

verifiedFacts.claim: Stevie Wonder told Musician magazine that he wrote "I Wish" on the day of a Motown picnic in the summer of 1976, going to Crystal Recording Studio right afterward where the vibe came to him from running at the picnic and the contests.

sourceRefs.extract: The day I wrote it was a Saturday, the day of a Motown picnic in the summer of ’76,” he told Musician magazine. “God, I remember that because I was having this really bad toothache, it was ridiculous. “I had such a good time at the picnic that I went to Crystal Recording Studio right afterward and the vibe came right to my mind, running at the picnic, the contests, we all participated. It was a lot of fun, even though I couldn’t eat the hot dogs – that was around the time of the creation of those chicken hot dogs. And from that came the ‘I Wish’ vibe.”

verifiedFacts.claim: "Pastime Paradise" opens with a fugue that borrows its first eight notes from Bach's Prelude No. 2 in C Minor, was intended to mimic the Beatles' "Eleanor Rigby," and features Hare Krishna chanting on the fade out.

sourceRefs.extract: The latter opens with an insistent cartwheeling fugue that borrows its first eight notes from Johann Sebastian Bach’s “Prelude No. 2 in C Minor.” Intended to mimic the Beatles’ “Eleanor Rigby,” the anxious instrumental phrase is made even more disorienting by the sound of a backwards gong that anticipates the chanting of Hare Krishnas heard on the fade out.

sourceRefs.extract: “Isn’t She Lovely” – a joyous celebration of parenthood – is perhaps the most obvious beneficiary of Wonder’s new inspiration. verifiedFacts.claim: Rolling Stone reports that the lyrical location was originally “Saginaw,” intended as homage to Wonder’s Michigan birthplace, before the song shifted into outer space after a guitarist misheard the title as the ringed planet.

sourceRefs.extract: The lyrical location was originally “Saginaw,” Wonder’s Michigan birthplace, and intended as homage to his home in the mold of the Jackson 5’s “Goin’ Back to Indiana.” But the song was shifted into outer space when guitarist Mike Sambello (later to score a hit with the Flashdance favorite “Maniac”) misheard the title as the ringed planet.

sourceRefs.extract: Some even believe that “Ebony Eyes” – with its reference to a “Miss Beautiful Supreme” – is an ode to Wonder’s childhood infatuation with elder Motown labelmate, Diana Ross. “I had a crush on her,” he admitted to Vanity Fair in 2008. “When I came to Motown, she walked me around the building and showed me different things – she was wonderful.”
